utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. May I first ask the parties whether their meeting of yesterday afternoon brought any result which is important enough to inform the Chamber about? Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for giving the floor to the Defence. The Defence would like to very briefly tell you something about the discussions that we had yesterday afternoon, if you will allow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as a matter of fact, we did have a meeting with the representative of the Prosecution yesterday, and unfortunately, if there is any progress, it isn't considerable. What the Defence can propose that would be acceptable is the following: Is that the witnesses, as they come here to testify, they could come with a statement where they would actually read the basic information, that is, all personal data, the names, date of births, addresses, dates of any stays if there are any in Sarajevo or any other cities, then the duties, the functions that they had, and also, the names of people that they were able to contact in Sarajevo as part of their activities. Moreover, any more than that, the Defence could not accept and that the reason is the following: We saw that a large number of written statements were prepared by the Prosecution, and as the Defence and the Chamber can know of course how these statements were prepared, made, and if we accept the tendering, just a simple reading of a statement which has been pre-prepared, that would be completely opposed to the sacrosanct principle of the quality of arms and debate. Now, why does Defence think that? We can just refer ourselves to a recent example, Witness J, that we had yesterday. We still remember very well the testimony of that witness before the Chamber and you saw, Mr. President and Your Honours, to which an extent the statements are important. Now, this witness spoke about his brother who wasn't yet 18 and he spoke about this brother in an ambiguous way, about possible membership of his brother in a military unit. Now, the Defence would never have been able to ask questions that they did ask if this was -- if he was not there. So it is very important to find out about why a child would be near a military installation if we only had a reading of a statement. Why is that? Because when we are reading, reading a text which has been pre-prepared by one of the parties in the case, there is no such a thing as testimony present. So it would be -- it is not quite an oral copy of the statement. So that is why this is not possible. So in order to speed up the proceedings, and the Defence would like to do that, but I don't think we want to really create a short cut. If we create a short cut, what we are going to amputate would be the rights of the Defence to a fair trial. And the Defence is very well aware that this is perhaps just a formal question, however, we know to which an extent, even if a form is not essential, it is still a very important and a determining factor. Now, Mr. President, if a rule or rules that are applicable to this procedure can prevent the testimonies, that is because we want something else. We want because the witnesses can testify before this Chamber. Just reading the statements would not be anything else but just tendering the statements, the written statements, and I believe neither you nor the Defence would have the possibility to really cross-examine the witnesses. And that is the reason why we believe that this is not admissible. And there is also another reason. What we fear, Mr. President, is that we would then be using this case for other cases, and this is why the Defence has to indicate here that in the statement for Mr. Magnusson that we have read on some 10 pages, there are only three or four passages that relate to General Galic, more or less. Everything else is really of interest to other people that are not concerned with this -- these proceedings, neither directly or indirectly. So this is not even to do with possible subordinates of General Galic. So what the Prosecution is trying to do is to find certain weapons, so to speak, on the basis of Article Rule 92 bis, and this is not really gaining time if we proceed in this fashion. Now, we know that the form is not essential, that is perhaps the determining factor, but what the Prosecution is trying to do with this is not to gain time, but to create a short cut and to cut off some rights from the Defence, and that is the reason why the Defence does not agree with this way of proceeding. Another point I would like to raise, and I am sorry I have to do it now, but that is the following: The Defence has to oppose another point, it is a different point completely, and we have to oppose the way that a part of these proceedings is being conducted -- not the way it is conducted, but the way it is proceeding. Now, my co-counsel and I were trying to spend a lot of time preparing for an important witness that we were told would be on the 6th of May, and that was supposed to be Mr. Richard Mole, and he was supposed to come on the 14th, 15th, 16th of May, and -- or 6th of May, for some six hours of testimony, and this was supposed to be a very important witness. And the Defence spent a lot of energy preparing for this witness. Perhaps we spent more energy for him than for other witnesses. Now, yesterday we received a letter where it said that, let's forget Richard Mole, that will not happen next week. We don't know exactly when he will come, but then we are then given another list of names and witnesses. 7th of May was yesterday and now it has been days that we have been preparing ourselves for Richard Mole. We haven't had time to prepare ourselves for other witnesses, and now this is even a more basic question. This is a very important matter. The Defence must be able to prepare itself and if they are not -- if they cannot prepare themselves, if they are told at the last minute, "Just forget what you have been doing so far; perhaps later we will come to this Witness" after you forgot about your preparation. The Defence cannot accept it. General Galic cannot accept this, considering that there is -- there are problems of communication before the Defence and General Galic, who is still in detention. Now, what the Defence would like to ask now, considering the state of health of General Galic - although perhaps we will speak about it a little later - now, what the Defence would like to have is a break in the proceedings in order to be able to prepare for these further witnesses as they were communicated by yesterday, 7th of May, because this has greatly upset the order of the witnesses. And I think we would need a break in the proceedings for about ten days so that we can be absolutely certain and prepared to -- for the Defence to do what they are supposed to do, and that is to defend their client. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, would you respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, I will respond. It appears that I have singularly failed to communicate to the Defence at our meeting yesterday accurately what I had in mind in relation to the reading of statements, because what my friend has said about that proposal is not at all what I thought I had said. Mr. President, what I proposed was that witnesses read the relevant part of their statement out loud in examination-in-chief. That would save some time because the interpreters would, of course, have a copy of the marked relevant passages in the booths, and in that fashion, we could save valuable minutes, at least, in getting the relevant parts of the evidence before you in chief. Not for a minute did it occur to me that the Defence would interpret that as a means to deprive them of cross-examination of the witness in relation to the passages they had read. But it would seem from what my friend has said that that was the impression he walked away with. Of course, if that had been my suggestion, that would have been subverting the very purpose of Rule 92 bis. But to be clear on it, and perhaps my friend can be assisted by this, that is not what I proposed. It is certainly not what I intended to propose. So perhaps he could at some point, either today in court or later at a meeting, indicate what his position is in relation to witnesses simply being invited to read the relevant portions of their statements, perhaps with some modification, where required, by further questioning on the part of the Prosecution and then, of course, we would move to cross-examination. Mr. President, I concur with my friend that there was not much that came out of yesterday's meeting, unfortunately. We did our best to creatively develop some proposals to put to you, but we were unable to do that. In relation to the calling of Mr. Mole, my friend said that we wrote him a letter yesterday and told him to forget about Mole. Indeed, we did send a letter, but in that letter, we said -- noted that we are scheduling Richard Mole to appear for a later date. That, of course, was not done, for arbitrary reasons. We had a difficulty at the last minute yesterday in securing Mr. Mole's attendance. It was beyond our control. It had to do with Mr. Mole's commitments. And that meant we had to then reschedule him, which we have done for the 3rd of June. I am pleased that my friends have prepared their cross-examination of him because, hopefully, that will assist them in dealing with Mr. Mole when we do call him. I regret it. I appreciate that it is difficult for the other party when there is a last minute revision of the order of witnesses, but I assure you, Mr. President, and I assure the Defence, it was not done arbitrarily, and it is probably fair to say that in this last quarter of the Prosecution case, that sort of problem, in spite of all our best efforts, is likely to occur because of the nature of the occupations of many of the witnesses that we are calling in this last segment. We will do everything that we can to avoid that. Mr. President, that brings me to the list of witnesses that the Prosecution intends to call in the remainder of the case. Yesterday, I anticipated that this morning I would make available to you a list of witnesses and, in essence, a proposal as to how the Prosecution would complete its case within the time limit that you have set of the 5th of July. I have given to the Defence and to you, through the Registry, a list of witnesses still to be called, with some additional material. Perhaps, Mr. President, I could explain some things in relation to that list. Firstly, a minor matter, Witness number 38, of course, was called yesterday so that name should be removed. There should also be a revision of the total hours of examination-in-chief. That figure of 66 hours should be 64 hours. Mr. President, the list of 40 witnesses still to be called means that the Prosecution has deleted from its Rule 65 ter original list of witnesses some 63. You will note that the first half dozen or so witnesses are expert witnesses. I have included on the list an additional witness, that being Barry Hogan. His name has come up repeatedly during the Prosecution case thus far. And you would have noted that he is an investigator in the employment of the Office of the Prosecutor. His evidence is very much of a secondary nature during the sniping component. At various times there were some references to him. He appears in the video of the sniping and shelling incidents, and it is really more in the matter of housekeeping of various facts and figures and dates that he recorded, and I anticipate that there would be no problem, at least I would hope so, if his evidence was to be given by way of 92 bis. The same could be said for Zoran Lesic, who appears on this list at number 26. You will recall that he has already given some evidence in which he explained the modus operandi of the videoing and taking and editing and production of the 360-degree photographs. And I did make clear at that stage that I did propose to recall him. His evidence will be of a similar nature of that of Barry Hogan, in addition to which he will provide some information as to the time that the Office of the Prosecutor obtained possession of various video clips, including those which we used in the opening. For that reason, his evidence would seem to fit comfortably within the guidelines of Rule 92 bis, which means, Mr. President, that we are looking at 39 -- 38, 39 witnesses still to call to give evidence in the Trial Chamber. I have revised the estimates in respect of these witnesses, the estimates of the time that the evidence in chief would take in respect of all but the experts. With that qualification, it is something in the order of 64 hours. I note that from today, and including today, until the 5th of July, we have some 35 days of court time remaining for the Prosecution case. If one works on the basis of that translating as four hours per day, it means we have left 140 hours of court time. I hasten to add that for the days where we commence evidence in the morning at 9.00 and conclude at 1.45, I think in fact it is a little less than four hours, but perhaps that four-hour estimate will do for these purposes. If one multiplies the evidence in chief estimates of 64 hours by 2, working on the basis of the rule that cross-examination is restricted in time to that which the Prosecution took, we are left with figure of 128 hours, and it becomes clear that we have a margin of 12 hours, which would barely be adequate, and perhaps being more honest about it, would be inadequate to accommodate the various objections, motions, technical difficulties, and so on that we can anticipate over the remaining two months. In addition, that leaves us with the experts. The reason that I have not allocated them an estimate of evidence in chief is that I am hopeful that some, if not most, if indeed not all of them, can be dealt with in the same manner as we dealt with Robert Donia, the historian. In other words, ideally, the witness simply gives his or her name, acknowledges that they have prepared the relevant report, and then I sit down. In the case of Mr. Donia, the Defence required, I think it was two days, to cross-examine him. The Defence -- in order for us to come up with a -- as reliable estimate as we can, and by "we" I mean the Trial Chamber as a whole, it is necessary to factor in how much time the Defence thinks it will need. So, foreshadowing what I'm coming to, Mr. President, it seems to me that this is perhaps a two-stage process. I anticipate that all of the expert reports will be filed by this Friday. If we are unable to meet that deadline in relation to one or two, I should imagine I will have them all filed by Monday or Tuesday. If there is any problem beyond that, at least I assure you that we will have a draft report filed. I do not expect a problem. The Defence under Rule 94 bis then has up to, and I stress those two words, 30 days to indicate its position. I wonder whether the Defence could look, at least in a preliminary fashion, at the reports when they are filed and provide to the Trial Chamber at least an estimate by, say, the end of next week, if not earlier, of how much time it thinks that it will need, Defence will need, to cross-examine those witnesses. Then perhaps we could arrive at a more realistic overall figure for the Prosecution case. Essentially, this particular problem underscores the difficulty that the Prosecution has in this jurisdiction of estimating the length of its case, as it is required to do in this jurisdiction. Simply put, the -- there is -- the solution does not rest with the Prosecution entirely. There is a variable factor and one which is controlled by the Defence, and that is putting to one side unexpected factors which have nothing to do with either party. So, Mr. President, expert witnesses aside, we have restructured the Prosecution case in a way which would be completed, if not by the 5th of July, then shortly thereafter but, of course, that does not take into account cross-examination of the experts. It may, of course, be that the Defence does not wish to cross-examine any of the experts, but I would be surprised if that was the case. I wonder if there is anything else I can assist you with, Mr. President. Perhaps I should indicate as I did foreshadow yesterday, that there may be a minor change to the list of witnesses which I may be able to make clear by next Monday, and for reasons I would be -- much prefer to explain at that point rather than now, I should also make clear if it is not apparent, and it should be, that by numbering the list of witnesses still to be called, I do not mean to suggest that we would call them in that order. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is not intending to deal with all the problems, including a suggestion of a ten days break, et cetera, et cetera, right away. The thing we have to decide at this very moment is how we will proceed with the next witness. I mean, that is the first question that is in urgent need for an answer. Therefore, we will take a break of 10 minutes in order to confer with the Chamber, but, of course, not until after Mr. Piletta-Zanin has had an opportunity, or Mr. Ierace. So we will have a break anyhow soon on the question on how to proceed with the next witness and then we will deliberate on the other issues later today or tomorrow. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I am very sorry that my learned colleague didn't understand what I thought I indicated clearly. I spoke, in any case, in French. I was speaking about reading of written statements and it would not be, of course, reading the totality of the statement but, of course, of passages or perhaps whether it is half a passage or whole of the statement. This is -- the problem is the same. Some statements are three pages. Some are 15. This is a question of principle and it is also a question of form, but it is essential. We cannot say, I believe, that the Defence didn't understand the Prosecution's idea. Occasionally, the Defence does understand the ideas of the Prosecution. Perhaps the Defence can even anticipate the Prosecution's ideas. Rarely, that is true. But this hypothesis in the case of Mr. Magnusson that we will see soon -- when we read the statement, we saw that there are many things that have nothing to do with General Galic. There are only three paragraphs, I believe, on a whole of 14 pages, that have to do with General Galic. Now, Mr. President, I am at your disposal. I believe that I have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I respectfully intervene at this stage to remind my friend that Mr. Magnusson's evidence is to be given in closed court and it would therefore be inappropriate for him to refer to the contents of his statement

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think if you would have to discuss the content of the statement, it would. But I think you are just referring to the relevance of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] [In English] Thank you for this intervention. It was clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand it, you are just referring to Mr. Magnusson as part of his written statement being not directly relevant for the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That is exactly right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we don't have to discuss the content any further. May I just ask you a question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? If you look at Rule 94 bis, we see that the main issue, that is -- of course, that is about expert testimony, is the right of the Defence to cross-examine a witness on the evidence presented in chief, whether it is written or oral. You repeatedly told us that the right to a fair trial would be affected by reading part of statements. I think it is not in dispute that the Defence has a right to cross-examine the witness, whether he gave oral testimony or whether the evidence he gave was in a written form. Could you be more precise in explaining as in what way the rights of the Defence would be affected if the evidence in chief would be given in either by what you call a shortcut or at least in a condensed form? I mean, the whole scala is between asking a witness through non-leading questions, which would take a lot of time, up to the other end of the scala, where the witness just reads his prior written statement. Well, in this scala, we have to find perhaps a balance. Could you tell us that, apart from the right to cross-examine the witness, in what other way the rights of the Defence would be affected if in a condensed form the evidence would be given by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. President, thank you for these remarks. And I think I need to make two observations: The first would be to do with the Defence and the second would be to do with your Chamber, and I should start with the observations to do with your Chamber, but I would still start in logical way to do with the Defence. Now, first of all, if we take the example of Witness J that we heard yesterday, if Witness J had simply read his statement prepared by one of the parties, that is coming from one of the parties, that is the Prosecution, for instance: "I was not in the army. My brother, wounded or killed, was not in the army. However, I know that such and such an incident happened on such and such a date." We would never have been able, by looking at the witness, would not have been able to see or understand that there was a problem to do with what he was saying. So there is a huge difference between a reading of a statement that is done by one of the parties or what the witness is testifying about, so what he is going to say by himself rather than just repeating what has already been prepared. Now, that would - I am sorry to use this term - that would be a farce. But the second remark has to do with your Chamber. Now, we saw this witness and we saw something that was fundamental. There were children that were near, admitted into military premises for any reason. But this can explain a great number of things. This is the first time that we were able to discover through a testimony this matter. Now, without this testimony, we would never have been -- would never have been able to find out, nor would your Chamber, that children under 18 years were admitted near military premises if this witness by himself didn't say these things the way he saw them, the way he felt them, the way he knew about them. A simple reading wouldn't allow your Chamber to have this feeling of realty of things, a sense of reality. What I am talking about, a fumus veritatis, this kind of aroma of truth that you would not feel, had it not been for this witness speaking for himself. Of course, the Defence would not have been able to find out about it either. And this is just an example, but this is the example that we were all able to see yesterday. Now, if we look at it systematically throughout this case, throughout this trial, in other cases, in other trials, and obviously the game and the strategy of the Prosecution is to have these fragments that are happening developed in time and space in order to then have them duplicated in other cases, in other trials. I am talking about the Milosevic case, Plavcic case, other cases - it doesn't really matter - and basically these cases, these fragments, can then be repeated in other trials. They would be accelerated. There would be a short cut. I am talking about respect of principles, and not just one particular case. There are two aspects: There is this case with the example that we've just shown and also the whole procedure, as a general rule of international law. And I believe that I have been clear enough, Mr. President. At least, I hope that the Prosecution has understood what I said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I do understand you, while you say that the Defence would lose the advantage of starting with a live testimony rather than a written statement because that could give them a chance to cross-examine the witness on the wordings he used, the expressions he used, the flavour, I would say, of his testimony in court. May I also ask you: Could you provide the Chamber with any case law because, as far as this Chamber knows, approximately half of the world is starting with written testimony. I think, if I am thinking about the jurisdiction you come from, it is not very common that you start with a live testimony, but that -- I mean, it is not always. I know that you have a lot of criminal procedures in Switzerland, but it is not a general rule that you always start with an oral testimony in chief and that, on the basis of that oral testimony in chief, that you cross-examine the witness. At least, there are a lot of jurisdictions where you start with the content of the file and that, of course, there is a right to call those witnesses who have given written statements before and you examine them in court. Is there any case law that would entitle the Defence to start, as a beginning, as a basis of the cross-examination, with an oral testimony rather than the content of a file containing written statements? Is there any case law you could give to the Chamber to support the thoughts you just developed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this honour, Mr. President, if you think that I can spontaneously give you a case law example and, of course, I will look for it, and if I find it, I will give it to you. But I believe that this is not just a simple of question of how we start the procedure. This is a question of respect of the procedure that we have had in this trial. Although there could have been other solutions in other judicial systems, the question is also of respect of the continuity of the procedure that we have had so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am asking it specifically because you have told us that it would affect the fairness of the trial, and as we all know, in the Statute of the ICTY, we find, in this respect at least, a perfect copy of Article 6 of the European Convention of Fundamental freedoms and Human Rights, and which is almost again a perfect copy of Article 14 of the International Covenants on Civil and Political Rights. So therefore, since you invoked the trial would not be fair any more, if we would proceed otherwise, and since we all know that written statements as the start of the proceedings in the trial court are practiced widely, and since there is a lot of case law developed under Article 6 and Article 14, I wondered whether there was any case law which would demonstrate that this would be an unfair way of proceeding. I now do understand that you say it is the tradition in the ICTY that you are relying upon. We will take your observations into consideration. Is there any additional observation to be made, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President. The proposal that I put to the Defence yesterday was offered and made on the basis that if there was an agreement between the Defence and Prosecution, then that would overcome any jurisprudential hurdles that may exist within the Tribunal. I simply wish to express a note of caution as to whether, if we were to proceed to allow witnesses to read parts of their statement without the agreement of the Defence, then that would require a closer examination of the jurisprudence to see whether indeed it is permissible, and I would anticipate or, at least, interpret, Mr. President, your requests for assistance as perhaps indicating a similar concern. Mr. President, the second point I wish to make is that in relation to the manner in which the next witness will give his evidence, I am pleased that the Defence has proposed today that his evidence be given in effect in short form, anyway, in other words, he be taken to the relevant portions of his statement. And you may recall, Mr. President, that is precisely what I proposed yesterday. I explained that again in the meeting yesterday with the Defence, so I simply wish to make clear to you that there is no dispute from the Prosecution with that approach. In other words, even if Mr. Magnusson does not read the relevant parts of his statement, I anticipate that, everything going as I hope, it will be very short in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think then we need a couple of minutes for the Chamber to confer, so we will have a break of I would say approximately 10 minutes, 5, 10 minutes. Please stand by. --- Break taken at 9.47 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We did ask more of your patience than I indicated before, and it shows how difficult it is to give time estimates. On the other hand, we will give the parties a bit more guidance and not just on the witness to come. First of all, just reading out the statement of a witness is not a solution. In that respect, the Chamber thinks that the Defence is entitled to hear more from a witness than just to read out a statement. On the other hand, the Chamber welcomes if the -- at least, leaves it to the Prosecution to find a more efficient way, perhaps even a more condensed way, of presenting the evidence to be given by a witness. And the Chamber will be guided to a high degree by the subject matter of the evidence given in deciding upon any objections, if there are any. So it is mainly the subject matter that will guide the Chamber in its decisions on whether objections are justified or not. We will have to gain some experience with it. So we are not leaving, I would say, the traditional order, so there are no changes in the tradition of this Tribunal. But it's up to the Prosecution to find a practice which is efficient, which might be condensed, and we will then see what the subject matter is and then decide on whatever objection there might be made. The second issue is about the change of the order of calling witnesses. If there are major changes and if it is a witness who will testify for six hours, that is, as such, a major change, the Chamber wants to be informed right way from the very moment that it becomes clear that such a change is necessary. On the one hand, the Chamber does understand that it is very difficult for the Defence to change its preparations for the cross-examination from one moment to another; on the other hand, the Chamber also understand that the Prosecution is not in full control of the time of the witnesses it will call. One of the solutions is that while preparing the examination or the cross-examination of a witness, you should build in some flexibility. That is valid for both parties. That means that if I prepare for the cross-examination of a witness who will testify tomorrow and finish my preparations at 10.00 this evening, then there is no flexibility at all. If, on the other hand, you are working a couple of days in advance, you will be able to be more flexible. So that is, in general, an observation for the parties. The Defence asked for a break of 10 days. The Chamber will not grant such a break and, specifically, not for so many days, but whenever we are in a situation where the Defence says, "Because of the change of the order of calling witnesses, we are not able to prepare for Witness A, B, or C," then the Chamber would like to know specifically which -- on which witness the cross-examination could not be prepared. We will then consider when it was announced that there was a change of the order of calling these witnesses and we will then decide whether, in respect of that specific witness, there is any need to grant extra preparation time to the Defence. And then, of course, as you have experienced during the last few months, there are different ways of solving it, saying, "Well, we can't expect the Defence to cross-examine the witness now," or "We ask from the Defence that they would cross-examine the witness to the extent possible Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for this very moment and will grant extra time if needed." So the Chamber wants to be informed because the Chamber is fully aware of the problems, especially the change of the order creates for the Defence, and therefore we want to be informed if it comes to a specific witness. Then, of course, we are also better able to assess how much extra time you needed. For example, a witness which would take six hours to be examined in chief would be heard tomorrow although scheduled only in two weeks, that would ask for a different decision compared to the situation where a witness for one hour is scheduled for Thursday, would be changed with a second witness also scheduled for Thursday. So we want to take decisions in that respect in view of the specific situation where the Defence has indicated what time they would need for preparation. I indicated that we would only deal with the way we would proceed with the next witness, so the 20 minutes extra time we took we used to give you some guidance on the other issues as well. Is it clear to the parties what the Chamber intends to do? I see Mr. Ierace, for the transcript, you are nodding yes. For the Defence, Ms. Pilipovic, it is clear. Then before having the usual break, I would like to know - I don't know whether this can be done in open session or not - but is the Defence prepare to hear the examination-in-chief and is the Defence also prepared to cross-examine the witness scheduled for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is very grateful to you, Mr. President. We are prepared to continue carrying out our tasks and we are able to defend our client in the appropriate manner. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will do that. That means that I think it would be better to call Mr. Magnusson after the break, Mr. Ierace. I didn't hear that the Defence is not ready to proceed with the next witness, so that means that we will start after the break, in closed session, with the witness, Mr. Magnusson. There is one issue still to be dealt with at this very moment and that is the documents and exhibits we have seen yesterday when Witness J was examined. Madam Registrar, would you please guide us through these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3280.Z, video under seal; Exhibit P3279.ZZ, 360 degree movie, under seal; Exhibit P3234, map marked by witness bearing ERN number 02081029, under seal; Exhibit P3684, pseudonym sheet, under seal; Exhibit P3279.Z, photograph marked by witness, under seal; Exhibit D105, map marked by witness, under seal; Exhibit D106, map marked by witness; Exhibit D107, official report dated 4 September, 1993, in B/C/S, under seal; Exhibit D107.1, English translation under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am just checking whether D106 should be admitted under seal or not. I think there is no reason to do so. It is just marking on that map without any names or indications of. So that could be admitted not under seal. Mr. Ierace, I also saw P3119 on our list -- oh, yes, Mr. Mundis. The name sheet had a different number. I am just trying not to forget any of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the exhibit you didn't use?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is right, Mr. President, it was duplicitous, and to save time, we opted not to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that's clear to us now. Since there are no objections, they are all admitted in evidence, all under seal with the exception of D106. We will then start after the break in closed session. I suggest, if there is no major objections, that we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 11.04 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that we are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pages – 8119 –8176 – Redacted – closed session

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I repeat what was just said. During the last 10 minutes of the closed session where we should have returned into open session, it was verified whether the protective measures in respect of Witness R included voice alteration, as was not indicated on the list provided by the Prosecution. We have verified, by looking at the request of the 30th of October and by looking at the oral decision given on the 6th of December, whether voice alteration was requested and granted. It was. That means that we can't continue at this very moment. If there is any other issue to be raised by the parties, then it would be the appropriate time to do so, if it is at least a small issue. You raised already the grattage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. This is just in order not to waste time. Do we know whether tomorrow we are in here or in the other courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...this is what I wanted to indicate when we would adjourn. If that is the only issue to be raised, then we adjourn until tomorrow morning 9.00. Not this courtroom, but Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of May, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
